passage: When an old building is to be repaired, those responsible must first decide what, exactly, they are repairing it to. One answer, long popular and still widely held, is that the building should be returned to its original state, or to the state its first builders intended. Later additions are stripped away, missing parts are reconstructed from evidence or from informed guesses, and the result is a building more complete and more consistent than it has been for centuries. The appeal is obvious: the visitor sees the church or the fort as it was meant to be seen, whole and coherent.

The opposing answer holds that a building's history does not stop at its completion. A medieval hall that later acquired a Georgian window, a Victorian staircase and a twentieth-century kitchen is a document of all those periods, and to strip it back to its first state is to erase most of what it records. On this view the repairer's duty is to keep what has survived, to intervene as little as possible, and to make any new work distinguishable from the old, so that no one mistakes a modern guess for an original fact. The restored building, by contrast, presents the restorer's idea of the past as though it were the past itself.

I find the second answer more persuasive, but it is not as neutral as its defenders sometimes suggest. Not every layer is worth keeping: a cheap partition put up in a hurry may hide a painted ceiling of real importance, and refusing to remove it is itself a choice about which history matters. Keeping everything is also an interpretation, one that values continuity over quality and treats the accident of survival as a kind of verdict. The conservator, no less than the restorer, decides what the building will say.

What separates the two approaches, then, is not that one interprets and the other does not. It is that conservation, at its best, leaves its interpretations visible and reversible, so that a later generation with better evidence or different priorities can undo them. Restoration tends to make its choices permanent and to conceal them, since a convincing reconstruction is one in which the seams cannot be found. Because every generation has been confident about the past and most have been wrong about some of it, the approach that allows its mistakes to be corrected deserves the benefit of the doubt.

passage: A durable genre of business writing proceeds by a method that looks, at first sight, impeccably empirical. The author selects a number of companies that have performed outstandingly over a long period, studies them closely, and identifies the practices they share: a strong culture, perhaps, or a fierce attention to customers, or a willingness to abandon unprofitable lines. These practices are then offered as the causes of greatness, and the reader who adopts them is invited to expect something of the same result. The books sell well, partly because the companies are vivid and partly because the method appears to replace opinion with evidence.

The first difficulty is one of selection. By studying only the companies that succeeded, the method has no way of knowing how many companies followed the same practices and failed. If a great many firms had strong cultures and attended closely to their customers, and most of them disappeared, then these traits are not what separated the winners from the rest; they were simply common, and the winners, being a subset of the many, happened to possess them as well. The graveyard of failed firms is not consulted because it cannot easily be visited: failed companies leave few records, attract no researchers and give no interviews.

A second difficulty is subtler. Many of the traits that the method identifies are not observed independently of performance but described after the fact, by people who already know the result. A company that is doing well is said to have a bold strategy and a confident leadership; the same company, a few years later and in decline, is said to have been reckless and arrogant, though nothing in its conduct may have changed. The observers are not being dishonest when they do this; they are reading the same conduct in the light of what it later led to. Where descriptions of this kind are the raw material, the correlation between good practices and good results is partly manufactured by the way in which the practices were recognised.

Defenders of the genre have an answer to the first point: compare the successful firms with a matched set of less successful ones, drawn from the same industries and periods. This is a real improvement and should be acknowledged as such. But it does not remove the second difficulty, since the comparison firms are still described by people who know how they fared, nor does it settle a third, which emerges only with time. Several of the companies held up as models in such studies later stumbled badly, and the explanation usually offered is that they abandoned the principles that had made them great. That explanation can be given whatever happens. A theory that accounts for success by the presence of certain practices, and for failure by their supposed absence, has arranged never to be wrong.

None of this shows that the study of successful firms is worthless. Close accounts of how particular companies work can suggest hypotheses worth testing, and some of the practices they describe may well be beneficial. What the genre cannot do is what it most often claims to do: to identify, from the records of the winners, the reasons they won. A reader who wishes to learn from such books would do better to treat their lists of principles as questions rather than answers, and to remember that in a competitive market a large part of any outcome may be owed to timing and circumstance, which no one can copy.

passage: A scientific paper presents itself as a complete set of instructions. Its methods section lists the materials, the quantities, the temperatures and the timings, and the implicit promise is that anyone competent who follows them will see what the authors saw. This promise underwrites one of the most cherished ideas about science: that its knowledge is public, available in principle to anyone who can read, and independent of the particular people who first produced it. When a laboratory fails to reproduce a published result, the natural suspicion therefore falls either on the original claim or on the care of the people who tried to repeat it.

Anyone who has worked at a laboratory bench knows that the promise is only partly kept. Many techniques depend on skills that their practitioners cannot fully articulate: how firmly to tap a tube, how long a mixture should look cloudy before it is ready, which faint smudge on an image is signal and which is dirt. Such knowledge is not secret, and it is not mystical. It is simply of a kind that is acquired by doing and by watching others do, in the way that one learns to ride a bicycle rather than the way one learns a telephone number. A methods section can point toward it, but it cannot transmit it, any more than a manual can make its reader a competent cyclist.

It is not unusual for a group trying to build a new kind of instrument from published descriptions alone to fail again and again, while another group that has sent a member to spend some weeks in the original laboratory, or has received a visitor from it, succeeds, often without being able to say afterwards what the crucial difference was. In such cases the written instructions were not wrong. They were incomplete in ways that neither their authors nor their readers could have specified in advance, because the authors did not know which of the many things they did without thinking were the things that mattered.

Recognising this does not license complacency about how methods are reported. A great deal that is now left out of papers could be written down, and the habit of omitting it, whether to save space or to protect an advantage, deserves the criticism it receives. But the recognition does alter what we should expect from reform. Demanding ever longer methods sections will capture the explicit portion of a technique more fully while leaving the tacit portion exactly where it was. If the goal is that results can be checked by people other than those who produced them, some of the effort now spent on documents might be better spent on movement: on funding researchers to visit one another's laboratories, on recording procedures as they are actually performed, and on treating the training of a replicator as part of the cost of a replication.

There is a larger consequence as well. The picture of scientific knowledge as a body of public statements, detachable from the people who hold it, turns out to be an idealisation. Much of what a field knows lives in the hands of its practitioners and moves only when they do. This is not a reason to distrust that knowledge, since skills can be tested by their results as surely as statements can. It is a reason to treat the communities that carry it, and the slow work of passing it on, as part of the infrastructure of science rather than as a private matter of training.

passage: For most of the twentieth century, readers of newspapers paid only a fraction of what their papers cost to produce. The rest came from advertisers, who were buying not journalism but attention, and the arrangement was so familiar that few people thought about it. Readers believed that they were buying a newspaper; in commercial terms, they were the product being sold. When advertising money migrated to online platforms that could target audiences more precisely, many news organisations turned to the readers themselves and asked them to subscribe. The change has been widely welcomed, and with some reason. A publication that lives on subscriptions answers to the people who read it rather than to the firms that want to sell them things, and it has less incentive to chase the cheap, fleeting clicks on which online advertising depends.

Yet the subscription model carries a cost that its admirers tend to pass over. Advertising, whatever its faults, made news cheap for the reader and therefore widely shared. A wall that admits only paying readers divides the public into those who can afford careful reporting and those who cannot, or will not, pay for it. The second group does not stop reading. It turns to whatever is free, and what is free is increasingly material that is cheap to produce: opinion, aggregation, rumour and content funded by people with something to promote, whether a product, a cause or a candidate. The result is a two-tier system in which the quality of what one knows depends partly on what one spends.

This matters more for news than for most products because the value of good reporting does not stay with the person who buys it. A voter who is misinformed about a local budget affects the outcome for neighbours who read every line of it, and a neighbourhood in which most residents rely on rumour about a planning dispute will reach worse decisions, which the careful reader who paid for accurate coverage must then live with. In this respect news behaves less like a private purchase and more like public health: the well-informed are not fully protected if those around them are not.

The conclusion to draw is not that news should go back to an advertising model that has largely collapsed, nor that we should pretend that journalism can be given away without someone paying for it. Free news was never really free; its price was simply hidden in the cost of the soap and cars its advertisers sold. The question is how to keep the independence that reader revenue brings while limiting the exclusion it creates. Some answers are familiar: lifting the wall for stories of urgent public importance, cheaper access for students and libraries, and public or philanthropic support for reporting that markets will not fund. None is sufficient alone. But a news system should be judged not only by the quality of its best journalism but by how many people that journalism actually reaches.

passage: Along many mountain roads there are small paved areas where drivers are invited to stop, and a sign, often bearing the symbol of a camera, announces that a view is available. People get out, look, photograph and drive on. The arrangement seems so natural that its assumptions pass almost unnoticed: that the beauty of a landscape is something seen, that it is best seen from a particular spot, and that the right relation between a person and the land is that of a spectator standing before a picture.

These assumptions have a history. The habit of judging terrain by whether it composes well, with a foreground, a middle distance and a far horizon arranged as a painter might arrange them, was cultivated by travellers who had learned to look at scenery through the conventions of landscape painting, and some of them carried tinted mirrors or framing devices so that the real view would more closely resemble a canvas. We no longer carry such devices, but the camera and the viewpoint sign perform much the same function: they select, frame and fix. A landscape that cannot be composed into a pleasing rectangle tends, under this regime, to count as no landscape at all.

The costs are not merely aesthetic. Places that photograph poorly, a marsh, a stretch of flat scrub, a slow brown river, are more easily dismissed as empty and therefore more easily drained, cleared or built upon, even when they are richer in life than the dramatic gorge that everyone stops to admire. The spectator's posture, moreover, shrinks what nature has to offer. The smell of wet earth, the sound of insects, the feel of a slope underfoot and the slow change of light over an afternoon cannot be gathered from a lay-by in the two minutes before the engine is restarted, and a beauty that is only looked at from a fixed point is a beauty with most of its dimensions removed.

It would be ungrateful to dismiss the viewpoint altogether. For many people a framed view is where an interest in landscape begins; the sign that says 'look here' has taught countless travellers to look at all, and a habit of attention begun at a lay-by can grow into something larger. The trouble lies not in framing as such but in treating the frame as the measure of value. An appreciation of nature adequate to its object would have to include the unspectacular and the unframeable, and it would have to be practised on foot and over time, with the whole body rather than with the eye alone.

passage: The story is told in so many introductory textbooks that it has come to seem like common sense. Once upon a time, it runs, people traded goods directly: a farmer with grain who wanted shoes had to find a shoemaker who happened to want grain. Because such a coincidence was rare, someone eventually hit on the idea of a commodity everyone would accept, such as shells, salt or metal, and money was born. Credit and debt, in this account, come last, a refinement that becomes possible only once coins are available to measure what is owed.

The difficulty is that the story describes a world no one has found. Anthropologists who went looking for economies in which neighbours regularly exchanged goods by barter have, on the whole, come back empty-handed. What they found instead, in village after village, was something closer to running accounts. A woman who needs a pot from her neighbour simply takes it, and both understand that something will be owed; the debt may be repaid in grain at harvest, in labour at a wedding, or never precisely at all. Among people who expect to keep living beside one another, the problem of the double coincidence of wants scarcely arises, because no one needs the exchange to be completed on the spot.

Barter does occur, but in revealing places. It appears between strangers who do not expect to meet again, between groups who distrust each other, and among people who were once used to money and have been cut off from it, such as prisoners trading cigarettes or townspeople whose currency has collapsed. In each case barter is a response to the absence of trust, not the primitive condition out of which trust and credit later grew.

Defenders of the textbook story sometimes reply that it was never intended as history. It is, they say, a thought experiment showing why a medium of exchange is useful, and its value does not depend on whether any society actually passed through a barter stage. This is a fair point as far as it goes. But the thought experiment is not idle. By placing money first and debt last, it teaches us to see money as a neutral token that merely smooths trade between independent individuals, rather than as a way of recording obligations between people already bound to one another. If the record points the other way, the more natural conclusion is that money began as a method of keeping score.

passage: It has become common to describe the fashion for owning less, the bare room, the small wardrobe of good clothes, the ritual of discarding whatever does not earn its place, as a revolt against consumer society. Its advocates present it as a turn from having to being; its critics, when they bother, dismiss it as one more passing style. Both responses take the movement at its word, as a stance towards consumption. Neither asks what owning little communicates, which is a different question from what it intends.

At the end of the nineteenth century the economist Thorstein Veblen described how the wealthy display their standing through conspicuous consumption, spending visibly on what serves display rather than use. The sparse interior seems at first to invert his picture. Yet emptiness has its own costs, and they are not evenly distributed. A bare floor in a crowded city is a quantity of expensive space left deliberately unfilled. A wardrobe of a dozen garments presupposes that each is durable enough, and the owner's life predictable enough, to require no more. Above all, the confident discarding of objects depends on the assurance that they can be replaced when needed. Households that live close to scarcity keep things, the spare part, the old jar, the coat a size too large, because they cannot count on being able to buy them again; for them, accumulation is a form of insurance. To throw away freely is to display that one has no need of such insurance.

It does not follow that those who embrace minimalism are hypocrites whose real aim is to impress. That objection confuses motive with function. A practice can be sincerely chosen for its own reasons, calm, order, a dislike of waste, and still operate socially as a signal that its practitioners neither chose nor want. Many who pare down their possessions are doing exactly what they say. The point is rather that the meaning of a pattern of consumption is not fixed by the consumer's intention; it is fixed by what the pattern makes legible to others, and what restraint makes legible, in a society where most people cannot afford its preconditions, is security.

The more consequential lesson concerns the hope of opting out. If even refusal can be read as a position within the system of display, then consuming less is not, by itself, an exit from that system; it is a move within it, and often one available only to those already well placed. This is not an argument for consuming more. It is an argument for suspicion towards any claim that a change in private taste can amount to a social critique, since the field of taste has repeatedly proved able to absorb its own refusals and return them as distinctions.

passage: Arguments about the legacy of empire often take the form of an account book. On one side of the ledger are the railways, telegraphs, irrigation canals and universities that colonial governments built; on the other are the drained revenues, the famines, the suppressed industries and the humiliations of foreign rule. Defenders of empire add up the first column and find a surplus; its critics add up the second and find a debt. The exchange can continue indefinitely, because each side chooses what to count, and because neither can say what a fair price for a railway would be.

The deeper difficulty is that the ledger treats the items in the first column as gifts, things handed over to a population that would otherwise have lacked them. Consider the railway. In much of the colonial world, lines were laid out to connect mines, plantations and cotton-growing districts to the ports, and to move soldiers quickly to places where unrest might break out. Routes, gauges and freight rates were set according to the needs of export trade and military control, and the cost of construction was frequently met from local taxation or guaranteed by it. A railway designed in this way is not a present; it is an investment made by one party, with another party's money, for the first party's purposes. To enter it as a credit in the colonised society's account is to confuse being affected by something with being given it.

None of this means that colonial railways were useless to the people who lived alongside them. Passengers, often in numbers that surprised the companies, used the trains to visit distant shrines, to look for work in growing cities, to carry goods to new markets and, eventually, to travel to political meetings that the authorities would have preferred them not to attend. A technology built for one end was turned to others. But this point cuts against the ledger rather than in its favour, since the uses that mattered most to ordinary people were precisely the ones the builders had not intended and could not claim as their contribution.

What the account-book approach leaves out, then, is the question of who decided. A society that chooses to borrow money and build a railway, and gets the routes wrong, has made its own mistake and can learn from it. A society that has a railway built for it, on terms set elsewhere, has acquired a piece of infrastructure but not the habit of deciding about infrastructure. That second loss does not appear in any column, which is perhaps why the ledger has proved so durable: it allows both its defenders and its critics to argue about outcomes while ignoring the matter of agency altogether.

passage: Whether insects can suffer is a question on which serious people disagree, and on which the evidence is likely to remain inconclusive for a long time. Their nervous systems are tiny and organised very differently from ours; some of their behaviour looks like nothing more than reflex, while some looks uncomfortably like the behaviour that, in a dog or a bird, we would take without hesitation as a sign of pain. Faced with this uncertainty, the usual response is to treat it as permission. If we cannot know that insects feel anything, the thought runs, we need not worry about how we treat them.

This inference is much weaker than it looks. Uncertainty about whether a being can suffer is not the same as confidence that it cannot, and in other contexts we do not treat it so. A builder who is unsure whether a house is occupied does not demolish it on the grounds that no one has proved anyone is inside. What uncertainty calls for is a weighing: the probability that harm is occurring, multiplied by how bad the harm would be and by how many beings it would affect. With insects, the last factor is overwhelming. The numbers involved in agriculture, pest control and the growing industry that farms insects for animal feed run to many billions, so that even a modest probability of sentience yields a large expected total of suffering.

The obvious objection is that this style of reasoning proves too much. If any probability of suffering above zero, multiplied by a sufficiently large number of beings, can generate an overriding moral demand, then we might find ourselves obliged to reorganise our lives around bacteria, or around the remote chance that plants feel pain. That objection has force against arguments resting on probabilities so small that they amount to mere logical possibility. It has much less force here. The case for insect sentience is not a bare possibility of the kind that could be raised for any organism; it rests on specific behavioural and physiological features that insects share with animals whose capacity for pain we already accept, even if they share them only partially.

What follows is not that insects should be accorded the same consideration as mammals, nor that every crushed ant is a tragedy. It is that where we deliberately bring insects into existence in vast numbers and kill them, as in insect farming, we should prefer methods of rearing and killing that would minimise suffering if suffering is present, provided the cost of doing so is modest. Precautions of this kind ask little of us. To refuse them on the grounds that sentience has not been proved is to mistake the absence of certainty for the presence of a licence.

passage: In many large cities, a good part of the open space created in recent decades does not belong to the public at all. Developers are permitted to build taller or larger than the rules would otherwise allow on condition that they provide a plaza, an arcade or a garden that anyone may enter. The arrangement looks like an elegant bargain: the city gains open space without paying for it, and the developer gains floor area worth far more than the ground surrendered. Critics have long complained that the resulting spaces are often bleak, hidden or quietly discouraging, with benches too narrow to sit on and guards who appear the moment anyone lingers.

The usual form of the complaint is that these spaces are private, and that private space can never be truly public. This puts the matter in the wrong place. Ownership, by itself, settles very little. Many publicly owned squares are fenced at night, patrolled against skateboarders and stripped of seating to deter people who might sleep there, while some privately owned courtyards are generous, well kept and genuinely welcoming. If the test of publicness were the name on the title deed, we would have to call the first kind more public than the second, which is absurd.

What makes a space public is better described as a set of permissions: the right to be there without a reason, to stay without buying anything, to gather with others, to hand out a leaflet or to hold a placard. These permissions are exactly what private management is tempted to withdraw, not out of malice but because each of them is a small risk to the owner and none of them earns anything. A plaza can be open to all in the formal sense while being governed by rules, often unpublished, that make it public only for the well dressed and the briefly passing. The question to ask is therefore not who owns a space but who writes its rules, and to whom the writers must answer.

Seen this way, the bargain need not be abandoned; it needs to be completed. A city that trades floor area for open space is entitled to specify not only the dimensions of the plaza but the permissions that come with it, to publish them at the entrance, and to enforce them against owners as firmly as it enforces its building codes. Where it fails to do so, it has not acquired public space at all. It has paid, in floor area, for something that looks like a square and behaves like a lobby.

passage: An investigation that changes a law or ends a career is remembered for its result, and the result makes it look like a sound investment. The reporting behind it rarely looks that way while it is under way. A team may spend months requesting documents, cultivating reluctant sources and checking figures, only to discover at the end that the story cannot be stood up, or that it is smaller and duller than it seemed. No publication can know in advance which of its inquiries will succeed, so the cost of the one that does must also cover the many that quietly fail. Editors who have watched a promising inquiry collapse after half a year learn caution, and caution, in a publication under financial pressure, usually means fewer inquiries.

This uncertainty would matter less if the rewards of success flowed back to the publication that paid for it. Mostly they do not. Once a finding is published, rivals can report it within hours, and the citizens who benefit from a cleaner tendering process or a safer bridge are seldom the readers who bought the paper that exposed the problem. In the language economists use, the work produces benefits that spill over to people who did not pay for them, and goods of that kind tend to be supplied in smaller quantities than a society, if it could choose collectively, would want.

The most important of those benefits is also the least visible. Officials who know that their accounts might one day be examined behave differently from officials who are sure that they will not be. A local administration that expects a reporter to read its contracts has a reason to keep them clean, and the corruption that never takes place leaves no story behind it. The contractor who decides not to inflate an invoice, because a reporter once asked awkward questions about a neighbouring council, will never appear in any account of what journalism has achieved. Investigative journalism therefore works partly as a deterrent, and like other deterrents it is judged unfairly by its visible output; a quiet year may be evidence of its success rather than of its irrelevance.

Admirers of the form sometimes overstate its virtues. Investigations can be mistaken, and a reporter convinced of wrongdoing may read ambiguous evidence in only one direction, with real costs for the people named. Nor is every exposure a public service; some are driven more by rivalry or an appetite for scandal than by any public interest. But the case for supporting such work does not depend on its infallibility. It depends on presence. Deterrence works only if the possibility of scrutiny is continuous; a single celebrated exposure every decade, however brilliant, does less to discipline the powerful than a modest but permanent habit of looking. Those who fund journalism, whether readers, donors or the public purse, should therefore value a steady capacity for inquiry above the occasional prize-winning scoop.

passage: The claim that language shapes thought has had an unusual career. In its strong form, the view that the categories of one's language set the limits of what one can perceive or conceive, it was once fashionable, then thoroughly discredited, and it is now defended by almost nobody. The objections are familiar. Speakers of languages that lack a word for some distinction can usually learn to make it when they need to; translation, though imperfect, is possible; and people routinely think thoughts for which they struggle to find words. If a language were a prison, its inmates would not so regularly be found outside the walls.

From the ruins of the strong view a weaker one has been rebuilt, and the evidence for it is more respectable. Colour has been the favoured test case, because the spectrum is continuous while languages divide it differently: some have only a few basic colour terms, others a dozen. In one well-known kind of experiment, speakers of a language that has separate basic words for lighter and darker blue were found to be slightly quicker at telling apart two blues that fell on opposite sides of that boundary than two blues on the same side, while speakers of a language with a single basic word for blue showed no such advantage. The effect was modest, but it was there, and it seemed to show that words reach down into perception.

What the same line of work also found, however, is more revealing than the effect itself. When participants performed the colour task while silently rehearsing a string of digits, which occupies the verbal system, the advantage largely disappeared, whereas a comparable task that occupied spatial memory instead left it intact. The words, it seems, were not permanently altering how the visual system sorted colours. They were being used, there and then, as an aid to the task, recruited on the spot and set aside when the verbal system was busy elsewhere.

Defenders and critics of linguistic relativity have both tended to miss what this implies. The defenders read such results as vindication: language shapes thought after all. The critics read the smallness of the effects as deflation: language barely matters. But the finding fits neither reading well. It suggests that language does not so much reshape a mind that would otherwise be neutral as serve as one of the instruments a mind reaches for while it works. On this picture the interesting question is not whether a speaker's language has engraved its categories on her perception, but how often, and in which tasks, thinking proceeds by borrowing words as tools. That question is in one respect more modest than the relativists' and in another more radical, since it implies that much ordinary thought is partly carried out in language even where we take it to be wordless.

passage: Public discussion tends to treat time alone as a problem to be solved. Loneliness is described, rightly, as a source of real suffering, and the remedies proposed, from neighbourhood programmes to ever more ingenious ways of connecting online, share an assumption: that the less time a person spends unaccompanied, the better. On this view solitude and loneliness are a single condition seen from two angles, the first merely a polite name for the second.

The assumption confuses a fact about circumstances with a fact about experience. Loneliness is the painful sense that one's connections are fewer or thinner than one needs; it can be felt in a crowded room, and some of its most persistent forms occur within marriages and among colleagues who see each other every day. Solitude is simply being alone, and its quality depends on what one brings to it. For someone who is lonely, an empty evening confirms a lack. For someone who is not, the same evening may be the only time in the week when attention is not divided, when a thought can be followed to its end, or when grief or pleasure can be felt without being performed for anyone.

Many traditions have valued this second kind of aloneness. Hermits, monks and contemplatives have sought it deliberately, sometimes for years at a time, and periods of withdrawal into wilderness or retreat recur in the stories told about religious teachers in very different cultures. One need not share their aims to see the point they grasped: a person who can never bear his own company depends on others in a way that makes his relationships less free. Friendship is richer between people who could survive without it.

This is not an argument for withdrawal. Solitude is good largely because it is chosen and because it comes to an end; a solitude imposed by exclusion, or one that stretches on with no prospect of return, turns into the very loneliness from which it was supposed to be distinct. Nor is the capacity to be alone a substitute for company; it is a companion skill to it. But if the two conditions really are distinct, then policies and technologies that aim only at reducing time spent alone may, without anyone intending it, crowd out a good that most people need in some measure and few are ever taught to use. The cure for loneliness is better connection, not the abolition of solitude.

passage: The usual story of standard time is a story of order arriving to rescue confusion. Before the railways, we are told, every town kept its own time, set by the sun at its highest point, so that a clock in one town might differ by several minutes from a clock in another only a short distance to the west. Travellers were bewildered, timetables were impossible, and the adoption of uniform zones was simply common sense finally asserting itself. The story is not false, but it misdescribes what was replaced.

Local solar time was not a muddle for the people who used it. It was tied to something everyone could see: the sun reached its highest point at noon, and noon meant the same thing in the market, the place of worship and the field. For a community whose dealings were mostly with itself, there was little need to coordinate with anyone else, and a time that matched the daylight was the most sensible time to keep. The differences between towns became a problem only when goods and people began to move between them quickly enough for a few minutes to matter.

That is what the railways did. A train leaving one town and arriving at another an hour later could not be scheduled sensibly if each station kept its own noon, and on single tracks a mismatch of a few minutes could put two trains on the same stretch of line. Railway companies therefore began keeping a single time along their routes, and governments eventually followed them, dividing territories into broad bands within which every clock agreed. The change was not everywhere welcomed, and some towns resented being told that noon now arrived when a distant company declared that it had. Within each band, clock noon and solar noon could now differ noticeably, and in places at the edges of a zone they still do.

Nothing here suggests that standard time was a mistake. Coordinated schedules saved lives on the railways and made later systems, from telegraph networks to air traffic, workable. The point is that standardisation was not the discovery of a correct time hidden beneath local error. It was a choice to make clocks answer to a network rather than to the sky, made because the network had become more important to daily life than the position of the sun. To call the older arrangement confusion is to judge it by the needs of a world that had not yet arrived.

options.D: governments began to require one uniform time for keeping official records and collecting taxes.

passage: Few arguments about words are made with more confidence than the appeal to origins. Someone uses 'decimate' to mean 'destroy most of', and a correspondent points out that the word comes from a Roman military punishment in which one soldier in ten was put to death, so that its proper sense is the loss of a tenth. Someone else describes an idea as 'nice' and is reminded that the word once meant 'foolish' or 'ignorant'. The assumption in each case is that a word's earliest meaning is its real one, and that later senses are errors which happen to have spread.

The assumption cannot be applied consistently, and nobody tries. If original meanings were binding, 'nice' would still be an insult, and so would a good many words now used without a second thought; the critic who insists on the Roman sense of 'decimate' does not, as a rule, insist on the earlier senses of the other words in his own sentence. Nor is there any principled place to stop. Most words have a history that runs back past the language in which they are now used, and the 'original' sense of any word is simply the earliest one of which we happen to have records. To treat that sense as authoritative is to give a vote to speakers who have been dead for centuries and to deny one to everyone now alive.

What a word means is settled, as far as anything settles it, by how the people who use it understand one another. This is not a counsel of indifference, for a shift in meaning can have a cost: if a word that once marked a fine distinction comes to be used loosely, the distinction may become harder to express, and a writer may reasonably prefer to keep it. But that is an argument about present usefulness, and it has to be made on those terms. It gains nothing from the fact that the stricter sense came first.

Etymology is not thereby made worthless. The history of a word can explain an odd spelling, reveal a forgotten link between two words that now look unrelated, or show how a community's way of life left its traces in the vocabulary, and it is one of the pleasures of knowing a language well; what it cannot do is serve as a court of appeal. To know where a word came from is to know something about the past of a language; it is not to know what the word must mean today.

passage: For a long time the dominant attitude of academic history towards oral tradition was one of polite suspicion. A story passed from mouth to mouth over many generations, it was argued, must accumulate errors as surely as a manuscript copied by careless scribes, and in the absence of any original against which to check it, the historian had no way of telling the accurate parts from the embellishments. Against this, a more recent and more sympathetic current has insisted that societies without writing developed techniques of memorisation of extraordinary precision, and that their traditions deserve to be treated as archives in their own right. Each side, I want to suggest, misconceives the object it is arguing about.

The error both share is to assume that an oral tradition is trying to do what a written chronicle does, namely preserve a record of past events for its own sake, and to differ only on how well it succeeds. Traditions are rarely maintained for that purpose. A genealogy recited at the installation of a chief exists to establish that he is entitled to the office; an account of the first settlers exists to explain why one lineage holds the best land and another serves as its ritual guardians. Because the tradition answers to present needs, it changes when those needs change, and its changes are not random. Lines that no longer matter drop out; ancestors who connect currently allied groups acquire importance; the long, uneventful middle of the past is compressed, so that the founders seem only a few generations removed from those who remember their grandparents.

This is precisely why the sceptic's analogy with the copied manuscript is misleading. Random copying errors cannot be corrected without an original, but distortions that follow from a known function can, at least in part, be anticipated and read through. A historian who understands that a genealogy is a charter for office will be cautious about its middle generations and its convenient links, while attending closely to details that serve no present interest and are therefore unlikely to have been invented. Nor is all content equally fluid: formulaic songs, names of places and fixed ritual phrases are often transmitted with a fidelity that ordinary narrative never achieves, even when no one any longer understands what they mean.

None of this licenses the opposite romanticism. A tradition that is reliable about the shape of an ancient migration may be quite wrong about who led it, and no technique of memorisation can protect a story from a community's interest in retelling it. Written sources, it should be added, are hardly exempt from the same pressures; charters and chronicles were also composed to justify claims, and historians learned long ago to read them against the grain. Oral tradition, approached in that spirit, is neither an archive nor a fiction. It is a record of what a community needed its past to be, and that is itself a kind of evidence about the past.

passage: Archives were not assembled to answer the questions historians now put to them. A colonial archive records what an administration needed to know: revenue collected and revenue owed, disorders suppressed, petitions received and disposed of. The people it governed appear in its pages chiefly at the moments when they became a problem for the state, as defaulters, suspects, rebels or supplicants. A historian who reads such records along the grain, accepting their categories as descriptions of reality, will end up reproducing the administration's own view of the world, in which a refusal to pay becomes 'obstinacy' and a gathering at a shrine becomes a 'disturbance of the peace'.

The remedy most often proposed is to read against the grain: to treat the record as evidence of what it was designed to suppress or dismiss. A report that a village had refused its dues 'without any cause' can be read for the cause the clerk declined to set down. The insistence of officials, repeated across a dozen letters, that a rumour was baseless tells us that the rumour mattered a great deal to them, and probably to those who spread it. Fear, in such documents, is a kind of evidence. Practised with care, this method has produced some of the most illuminating social history of recent generations, restoring motive and intelligence to people whom the record had reduced to nuisances.

Yet the method has a limit that its enthusiasts sometimes forget. Reading against the grain still reads the grain. The voices it recovers belong to those who left a trace by colliding with power; those who never collided, who paid what was asked, married, worked their fields and died without incident, remain exactly where the archive left them, outside it. There is also a quieter temptation. When the record is thin, the historian's sympathies rush in to fill it, and the rebel recovered from the margins of an official report can look suspiciously like the rebel the historian set out hoping to find.

None of this is a reason to abandon the method. It is a reason to be candid about what it can and cannot do. A silence in the archive is not always a hidden voice waiting to be decoded; sometimes it is simply an absence, and the honest response is to mark it as one. Beyond that, the historian can turn to sources that were not produced by the same gaze: remembered songs and stories, the remains of houses and tools, the shape of fields and paths. The archive can be cross-examined with great profit, but it cannot be made to testify about what it never saw.

passage: For about a century after industrialisation, the working week in the richer economies shrank steadily, from something like sixty hours or more to around forty. Many observers assumed the trend would continue. If each generation could produce more in an hour than the last, it seemed natural that part of the gain would be taken as leisure, and confident predictions were made in the early twentieth century that the grandchildren of that era might work perhaps fifteen hours a week. In much of the rich world the decline instead slowed sharply after the middle of the century, and for many full-time professionals it appears to have reversed. The puzzle is not that people work at all, but that productivity kept rising while the hours of so many stopped falling.

The simplest explanation is that people chose income over time. Higher pay makes an hour of leisure more expensive, since each hour off now forgoes more, and it also makes people richer, so that they can afford more leisure. Which of these pulls is stronger is an empirical matter, and for a long period the second seemed to win. Perhaps, the argument runs, it simply stopped winning: people discovered new things to want faster than their incomes satisfied the old wants. A related account adds that much of what people buy matters to them chiefly in relation to what others have, so that a general rise in income buys no one a better position and the race to earn resumes at a higher level.

Both accounts treat hours as something workers choose, as they might choose how much bread to buy. That premise deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives. For most employees hours come attached to a job, and the menu of jobs is set largely by employers. A firm that pays a fixed cost for each person it hires, in recruitment, training, benefits and supervision, has good reason to prefer fewer people working longer to more people working less. In many professions, moreover, long hours have become a signal of commitment, and promotion goes to those who send it; a lawyer who would gladly trade a fifth of her salary for a fifth of her week may find that the trade is not on offer at all, or that it costs her far more than a fifth of her career. Under such conditions the hours we observe tell us what jobs offer, not what workers want.

The institutional account has a limitation of its own. It cannot easily explain why some people, given a genuine choice, still work very long hours, and it would be a mistake to deny that for many of them the work itself is the attraction. Nor are the averages uniform. In some economies the same decades that lengthened the week for well-paid professionals left many lower-paid workers with fewer hours than they wanted, pieced together from part-time or irregular shifts. An average that holds steady can conceal one group working too much and another too little.

What follows is that the old prediction failed less because of a mistake about human desire than because of a mistake about how labour markets work. The forecasters assumed that rising productivity would be divided between income and leisure by the free choices of workers. The division has in fact been made largely by the structure of jobs, and that structure can be altered: by rules on hours, by the way benefits are financed, by what firms choose to reward. Whether people would then work less is an open question, but it is one that the present arrangement prevents us from answering.

passage: During the twentieth century a movement grew up among performers of European music written before about 1800 that sought to recover how that music had sounded when it was new. Its adherents played on instruments built to older designs, or on surviving originals: harpsichords rather than modern pianos, gut strings rather than steel, wooden flutes without the elaborate keywork of later models. They studied treatises on performance written in the period and drew from them conclusions about tempo, ornamentation and the size of ensembles. Much of the result was a revelation. Textures that had sounded thick and heavy when played by large modern orchestras became transparent, and pieces long heard as dutiful exercises began to sound witty and alive.

The difficulty lies in the word that the movement often attached to itself, authenticity. If authenticity means sounding as the music sounded to its first audiences, the goal is in one important respect unreachable. Even if every instrument and every tempo could be reconstructed exactly, the listeners could not be. An audience that has heard the music of the following two centuries hears an older piece against all of it; a dissonance that once startled may now pass unnoticed, and a small ensemble that once seemed ordinary may now sound austere and pointed. The same sounds, entering differently formed ears, do not produce the same experience.

A second difficulty concerns the composers' own wishes. It is sometimes assumed that a composer who wrote for the instruments of his day would have wanted exactly those instruments, and that a performance on them is therefore more faithful to his intentions. But composers wrote for what was available, and some of them are known to have been dissatisfied with the instruments and players they had. To infer a preference from a circumstance is to confuse what a composer was given with what he would have chosen.

None of this tells against the performances themselves, many of which are among the most vivid of the past century. It tells against a particular way of justifying them. The best of these performances persuade not because they are correct, in the sense of matching a lost original, but because the research behind them led performers to hear possibilities that habit had concealed. Historical evidence used in this way is less a rulebook than a provocation: a reason to try something, which must then succeed or fail as music.

options.B: audiences came to prefer small ensembles to large orchestras for music of every period.

passage: Admirers of vernacular building, the houses and barns put up by people who were not architects, often describe them as stores of climatic wisdom. The thick earth walls of a desert village keep rooms cool through the afternoon and release their stored warmth at night; the steep roofs of a snowy valley shed their load before it can crush the rafters; the raised floors of a flood plain let the water pass beneath. Each form, on this account, is the answer a community reached after centuries of trial, and modern builders, with their sealed glass boxes and mechanical cooling, would do well to copy it.

There is much truth in this, but the story is told too kindly. The forms that survive to be admired are the ones that worked well enough to be kept; the failures, the houses that collapsed and the villages abandoned after a bad decade, left nothing for us to photograph. What we see is therefore a filtered record, and it flatters the past. More important, vernacular forms were shaped by poverty and scarcity as much as by climate. People built with earth because earth lay underfoot and cost nothing to carry, not because they had compared it with every other material and found it best. A thick wall may be cool, but it may also be dark, damp in the rains and laborious to patch every year, and those who lived behind it bore those costs whether or not their admirers mention them.

None of this makes vernacular building less worth studying. It suggests, however, that the lesson lies in the method rather than in the forms. What village builders did well was to adjust slowly and continuously to the conditions in front of them, keeping what worked and changing what did not, with materials whose behaviour they knew intimately because they handled them every season. Their knowledge was local by necessity, and its strength was precisely that it never pretended to be anything else.

A modern builder who copies the outward shape of a courtyard house in a different climate, with different materials and a different way of living, has learned nothing from it, however picturesque the result. One who studies local sun, wind and rain with the same patience, builds, watches what happens and is willing to revise, has learned a great deal, even if the building that results looks nothing like a village house.
